Extracting environmental data around observation points

Source: vignettes/articles/extracting-and-weighting-buffer-data.Rmd
extracting-and-weighting-buffer-data.Rmd

Environmental observations are often associated with a single location, depth and time. However, the conditions experienced by a marine animal may extend beyond that exact point. An animal may move between neighbouring cells, occupy several depths or encounter changing temperatures over time. Similarly, a longline may span several kilometres and remain deployed for hours. In these situations, we may want to describe environmental conditions around the recorded location, across relevant depths and over the duration of the event.

How can we summarise these conditions, and why might two averages of the same data give different results?

In this tutorial, we use extract_to_buffer() with a small example of Mediterranean Sea potential temperature. We build a buffer around one observation, compare two ways of calculating its mean, and look at the steps extract_to_buffer() runs for us.

Our research question

Imagine we have recorded a marine animal at:

  • Longitude 0 degrees and latitude 38 degrees.
  • A depth of 60 metres.
  • Midnight UTC on 20 September 2026.

We would like to describe the temperature within 10 kilometres of this location, between 50 and 70 metres deep, and from one day before to one day after the observation. Our question concerns a surrounding volume over time, not the single closest temperature value.

The data are a small netCDF subset of real modelled temperatures, included with this article, so no download or API credentials are needed. Their source is described at the end.

Getting started

The article files are in vignettes/articles/ in the source repository. When running these examples by hand, use that directory as your working directory.

library(ocean3d)

nc_file <- file.path("buffer-data", "temperature-subset.nc")
source(file.path("buffer-data", "figures.R")) # article_signature() below

We describe the file once with as_proxy(), which reads its grid, depths and time steps but no values. The file has no cell or depth bounds, so the edges of each cell and depth level are placed halfway between neighbouring centres.

temperature <- as_proxy(nc_file, var = "thetao")
temperature
#> class      : SpatProxy (experimental)
#> source     : temperature-subset.nc
#> variable   : thetao (degrees_C)
#> dimensions : 9 x 8 x 6 x 5 (lon x lat x depth x time)
#> lon        : -0.166666 to 0.166667, 9 cells, edges inferred
#> lat        : 37.8542 to 38.1458, 8 cells, edges inferred
#> depth      : 46.6522 to 72.6237 m, 6 levels, shallow first, edges inferred
#> time       : 2026-09-18 to 2026-09-22, 5 steps, standard calendar, no bounds
#> crs        : EPSG:4326

Our observation goes in a table. Longitude and latitude are decimal degrees, depth is in metres, positive downwards, and the time is in UTC.

observation <- data.frame(
  id = "observation_1",
  lon = 0,
  lat = 38,
  depth = 60,
  date = as.POSIXct("2026-09-20 00:00:00", tz = "UTC")
)
observation
#>              id lon lat depth       date
#> 1 observation_1   0  38    60 2026-09-20

Step 1: a weighted mean

A horizontal radius of 10 km gives a circle around the location. A depth radius of 10 m reaches from 50 to 70 m, and the time window runs one day either side, so the buffer is a cylinder from 50 to 70 m over 48 hours.

weighted <- extract_to_buffer(
  observation, temperature,
  horizontal_radius_km = 10,
  depth_radius_m = 10,
  time_before = 1,
  time_after = 1,
  output_col = "temperature"
)
weighted[c("id", "temperature", "temperature_n")]
#>              id temperature temperature_n
#> 1 observation_1     15.9614           450

temperature_n is the number of values the mean is built on: every grid cell the circle touches, at every depth level whose slab of water overlaps 50 to 70 m, on each of the three daily time steps in the window. A cell, level or time step counts in full once the buffer reaches it.

Each value is weighted by the volume of water its cell and depth level stand for. The depth levels in this part of the file thicken with depth, from about 4.7 to 5.7 m, so a value from a deeper level counts for a little more than one from a shallower level.

Step 2: an equal mean

Let’s repeat the extraction, changing only the weighting.

equal <- extract_to_buffer(
  observation, temperature,
  horizontal_radius_km = 10,
  depth_radius_m = 10,
  time_before = 1,
  time_after = 1,
  weighting = "equal",
  output_col = "temperature"
)

data.frame(
  weighting = c("weighted", "equal"),
  mean = c(weighted$temperature, equal$temperature),
  n = c(weighted$temperature_n, equal$temperature_n)
)
#>   weighting     mean   n
#> 1  weighted 15.96140 450
#> 2     equal 15.98204 450

The same values give two slightly different means. With equal weighting, every value counts once, so the thinner levels near the top of the window count as much as the thicker ones below. Here the levels differ little in thickness, so the means differ by only a few hundredths of a degree. Use the weighted mean for the average temperature of the water in the buffer, and the equal mean for the average of the grid values in it.

Step 3: the same steps written out

extract_to_buffer() is a shortcut for the build, intersect and summarise steps of an analysis. Written out, the weighted mean above is:

# Build: the observation as a 3D point, then a 10 km circle from 50 to 70 m.
point <- as_vector3d(observation, time = "date")
buffer <- buffer_3d(point, radius_km = 10, depth_window = 10)

# Intersect: read the cells under the buffer for each day in the window, and
# keep the values inside it.
days <- as_voxel(crop(temperature, buffer),
                 time = as.POSIXct(c("2026-09-19", "2026-09-21"), tz = "UTC"))
inside <- lapply(days, function(v) suppressMessages(mask(v, buffer)))

# Summarise: one row per day, or all three days together.
summarise_3d(inside)
#>         time     mean   n
#> 1 2026-09-19 15.97945 150
#> 2 2026-09-20 15.98180 150
#> 3 2026-09-21 15.92295 150
summarise_3d(inside, by = "all")
#>   time    mean   n
#> 1 <NA> 15.9614 450

The pooled row is the mean extract_to_buffer() returned. Writing the steps out is useful when the same buffers are summarised in several ways, or to see how the conditions change from one day to the next.

Step 4: other statistics

statistic also gives the standard deviation, the minimum or the maximum. Each call gives one statistic per observation.

statistics <- c("mean", "sd", "min", "max")
data.frame(
  statistic = statistics,
  temperature = vapply(statistics, function(s) {
    extract_to_buffer(observation, temperature, horizontal_radius_km = 10,
                      depth_radius_m = 10, time_before = 1, time_after = 1,
                      statistic = s)$thetao
  }, numeric(1))
)
#>      statistic temperature
#> mean      mean  15.9613974
#> sd          sd   0.3928506
#> min        min  15.4408598
#> max        max  17.1730785

The standard deviation describes the spread of the values inside the buffer. Values in neighbouring cells, levels and days are usually correlated, so it isn’t a measure of the mean’s uncertainty.

Step 5: buffers in fewer directions

A buffer doesn’t need to extend in all three directions. Without a depth window, method picks one depth level in each cell the circle touches. By default this is the level nearest the observation’s depth that has a value, as extract_to_point() does; "surface" and "bottom" take the shallowest or deepest level instead. Each cell then counts by its area. Without a time window, the time step nearest the observation is used.

data.frame(
  method = c("nearest", "surface"),
  temperature = c(
    extract_to_buffer(observation, temperature,
                      horizontal_radius_km = 10)$thetao,
    extract_to_buffer(observation, temperature,
                      horizontal_radius_km = 10, method = "surface")$thetao
  )
)
#>    method temperature
#> 1 nearest    15.91890
#> 2 surface    17.28152

When there is no value

An observation without a date, outside the grid, or with no time step in its window gets NA, and its _n column is 0. One warning counts these observations, by reason.

undated <- observation
undated$date <- as.POSIXct(NA, tz = "UTC")
extract_to_buffer(undated, temperature, horizontal_radius_km = 10)[
  c("id", "thetao", "thetao_n")
]
#> Warning: 1 of 1 observations get NA: 1 without a usable position, depth or
#> date.
#>              id thetao thetao_n
#> 1 observation_1     NA        0

To drop summaries built on too few values, filter on the _n column.

Summary

We have described the conditions around an observation with a horizontal, vertical and temporal buffer:

  1. We built a buffer around one observation.
  2. We compared a volume-weighted and an equal mean of the same values. Here they differ by a few hundredths of a degree, because the depth levels are similar in thickness.
  3. We wrote out the build, intersect and summarise steps that extract_to_buffer() runs.
  4. We calculated other statistics, and buffers in fewer directions.

Next steps

  • The workflow article shows the same steps for points, buffers, tracks and areas.
  • Use extract_to_point(), or terra::extract() on a SpatProxy, when the question concerns a single cell and level rather than a surrounding buffer.

Data sources and reproducibility

The example is a subset of Mediterranean Sea Physics Reanalysis, product MEDSEA_MULTIYEAR_PHY_006_004, dataset cmems_mod_med_phy-temp_my_4.2km_P1D-m_202511. It contains the original thetao values and coordinate centres from a download made on 19 October 2026. The original metadata identifies CMCC as the producer and describes the data as daily mean potential temperature.

E.U. Copernicus Marine Service Information; https://doi.org/10.48670/mds-00375. The subset retains this attribution. Source data remain subject to the Copernicus Marine Service licence. The article does not imply endorsement by Copernicus Marine or CMCC.

The article’s buffer-data/README.md records the subset and its preparation. The repository script data-raw/buffer-article.R regenerates the subset from the downloaded original. It keeps neighbouring coordinates, so the inferred edges match the larger file. It does not add bounds or alter the original temperature values.

All arguments and defaults

Expand or collapse the complete extract_to_buffer() signature

This signature is generated from the current function. Arguments without a default require input. Where a vector lists alternatives, its first entry is the default; supply one alternative in a call.

extract_to_buffer(
  # Data and sources
  data, nc, var = NULL,

  # Horizontal buffer
  horizontal_radius_km = 0,

  # Depth buffer
  depth_radius_m = 0,

  # Time buffer
  time_before = 0, time_after = 0,
  time_unit = c("days", "hours", "minutes", "seconds"),

  # Statistics inside each buffer
  statistic = c("mean", "sd", "min", "max"), weighting = c("weighted", "equal"),

  # Depth selection
  method = NULL,

  # Observation and output columns
  lon_col = "lon", lat_col = "lat", depth_col = "depth", date_col = "date",
  output_col = NULL,

  # Source columns and dimensions
  lon_dim = NULL, lat_dim = NULL, depth_dim = NULL, time_dim = NULL,

  # Temporal selection
  time_match = c("nearest", "exact"), max_time_diff = NULL
)

See extract_to_buffer() for units, accepted inputs and the complete return description.
